title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
status: Retrieved and read from the publisher or research author’s GitHub source
claim: The study repository reports a 0.188 ratio-minus-one estimate: approximately 18.8% more time with AI access. Its published data contains 246 issues and 16 unique developers.
scope: A randomized study of experienced open-source developers using early-2025 AI tools on their own repositories.
caveat: This is not an estimate for beginners, every developer, all tasks, or later AI tools. Repository README and sample counts were verified; this task did not reproduce the regression. It does not measure hiring demand.
implications: Measure quality and time on matched tasks before assuming an AI productivity gain.
Require unaided explanation, debugging, tests, and reproduction alongside AI-assisted work.
excerpt: 0.188 = E(Time with AI) / E(Time without AI) - 1

title: OpenAI Evals

title: Common pitfalls and recommended practices
published: Living documentation; no single publication date established
status: Retrieved and read from the publisher or research author’s GitHub source
claim: Information unavailable at prediction time creates data leakage and optimistic evaluation. Fit preprocessing only on training data; pipelines help keep transformations correctly scoped.
scope: Primary documentation for reliable conventional ML evaluation.
caveat: Random splitting is not sufficient for every data-generating process; time, entity grouping, and deployment context still require reasoning.
implications: Teach train/validation/test boundaries before model selection.
Require a leakage audit, an appropriate split, a baseline, and held-out evaluation in the first ML portfolio project.
excerpt: The general rule is to never call fit on the test data

title: Deep Learning Tuning Playbook
published: Living document; no single publication date established
status: Retrieved and read from the publisher or research author’s GitHub source
claim: The playbook frames tuning as a scientific process: choose experimental goals, design runs, track results, inspect failure modes, and consider compute costs.
scope: Practitioner guidance focused on supervised or similar deep-learning training.
caveat: The authors explicitly describe it as their evolving opinions, not an objectively optimal recipe or supported Google product.
implications: Teach hypothesis-driven experiments and one interpretable intervention at a time.
Log seeds, data versions, configurations, curves, budget, and unsuccessful runs.
excerpt: This document represents the opinions of the authors at the time of writing, not any sort of objective truth

title: vLLM: inference and serving
published: Living repository; foundational PagedAttention paper cited as 2023
status: Retrieved and read from the publisher or research author’s GitHub source
claim: The serving project documents KV-memory management, continuous batching, quantization, streaming, distributed inference, structured output, and tool calling.
scope: Primary implementation documentation for LLM serving.
caveat: Supported features and hardware evolve. Feature lists and contributor counts are not employment statistics. Learn serving tradeoffs before committing to a framework.
implications: Measure latency distributions, throughput, memory, quality, and cost together.
Treat distributed inference and GPU kernels as a later systems specialization.

title: OpenAI Agents SDK
published: Living repository; no single publication date established
status: Retrieved and read from the publisher or research author’s GitHub source
claim: The SDK exposes tools, handoffs, input/output guardrails, human involvement, sessions, and tracing as explicit workflow components.
scope: Primary documentation for one agent framework.
caveat: A feature is not a guarantee of safety or usefulness. This does not establish that every product needs agents or this SDK.

Compare an agent against a simpler deterministic or retrieval workflow on the same evaluation set.

title: MLOps with Vertex AI
status: Retrieved and read from the publisher or research author’s GitHub source
claim: The end-to-end sample separates dataset management, model development, pipeline tests and deployment, continuous training, serving, monitoring, and metadata tracking.
scope: Primary older educational implementation of an ML lifecycle.
caveat: The source states it is not an official Google product and has outdated dependencies. Use its lifecycle concepts, not its old install commands. It does not prove current cloud market share.
implications: Teach data validation, reproducibility, CI/CD, serving, monitoring, and rollback as separate responsibilities.
Use local tools first; map the same responsibilities to one cloud only when a project needs it.
excerpt: Run unit tests; Run a local e2e test of the TFX pipeline

title: How Adaptable Are American Workers to AI-Induced Job Displacement? — replication package
published: 2025 paper attribution in repository; repository inspected 2026-10-28
status: Retrieved and read from the publisher or research author’s GitHub source
claim: The author-maintained replication package constructs occupation-level adaptive capacity conditional on AI displacement; it distinguishes exposure from workers’ ability to adapt.
scope: United States occupation-level research using SIPP, O*NET, OEWS, ACS, and other sources described in the repository.
caveat: This task verified the README and provenance metadata, not the full paper or results. It does not predict the user’s job outcome and cannot be generalized directly to a global market.
implications: Separate task exposure, adoption, displacement, hiring, and individual employability.
Build transferable software, statistics, communication, and domain skills as a hedge against changing tools.
